title: Barnard's Star — the fastest-moving star in our sky
plain_result: Subtract the later pictures (Mar–May 2026) from the earlier ones (Aug–Oct 2025) and this star shows as an orange–blue pair. By eye, its light has moved north, as Gaia predicts; we do not turn this picture into a number, and it is made from the experimental colour-aware pictures (open the live view below). Measuring its speed from SPHEREx positions did not work: we get -5.0 ± 1.9″ and +5.6 ± 1.5″ per year, against Gaia's -0.80″ and +10.36″ (likely cause, untested: the star saturates SPHEREx's detector, so the fit rests on its outer light; only two time windows are available; What failed #13).

evidence_links.text: Why the motion fit fails: What failed, item 13

method_note: The picture: the tool splits the pictures at the largest gap in time and subtracts the later set from the earlier one, using the experimental colour-aware pictures. The motion fit: likely cause of the failure (untested) is saturation — saturated pixels are masked, so the position rests on the star's outer light; Gaia's parallax is held fixed.
